The 3 Master Rules That Unlock Everything

Rule 1: The Magic Number 8 (The Octet Rule)

Every atom in the universe wants peace and stability! To achieve this, it wants its outermost valence shell to hold exactly 8 electrons (like noble gases Neon and Argon).

Key Takeaway: An atom with 1, 2, or 3 valence electrons gives them away. An atom with 5, 6, or 7 takes them!

Rule 2: Metals vs Non-Metals Personality

Metals are Generous Givers: They lose valence electrons easily to become positive ions (Cations like Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺).

Non-Metals are Hungry Takers: They snatch electrons to become negative ions (Anions like Cl⁻, O²⁻, N³⁻).

Memory Anchor: Metal = Generous donor (+) | Non-metal = Greedy borrower (-)

Rule 3: The "Sea of Delocalised Electrons"

Why don't metals shatter when hit with a hammer? In a metal, positive nuclei float inside a fluid "sea of free electrons". When hammered, the layers slide past each other smoothly without breaking bonds!

Secret Reason: This free electron sea explains Malleability, Ductility, Electrical Conductivity, and Metallic Shine all at once!

Why is Hydrogen [H] in the metal reactivity series?

Hydrogen is a non-metal, but like metals, it can lose an electron to form a positive ion (H⁺). All metals ABOVE Hydrogen displace H₂ gas from dilute acids. Metals BELOW Hydrogen (Copper, Silver, Gold) cannot!

The "Chemical Bully" Rule (Single Displacement)

A metal higher up on the ladder is stronger (more reactive). When placed in a solution of a weaker metal, it kicks it out! Fe + CuSO₄ (blue) ➔ FeSO₄ (pale green) + Cu (reddish brown)

Paradox #1: Alkali Metals

Why Sodium & Potassium are Kept Under Kerosene

Sodium (Na) and Potassium (K) are super reactive. If left in open air, they react vigorously with both oxygen and moisture, releasing H₂ gas which instantly catches fire. Because they do not react with hydrocarbons, they are safely preserved submerged in kerosene oil.

Paradox #2: White Phosphorus

Why White Phosphorus is Stored Under Water

White phosphorus (P₄) is a non-metal with an ignition temperature of just 35°C. In summer, room temperature alone can make it spontaneously burst into dense toxic white fumes (P₄O₁₀). However, phosphorus does not react with water, so it is permanently stored submerged under cold water!

Fundamental Properties

Physical Properties & The 10 Famous Anomalies

Mastering mechanical, electrical, and thermal behavior plus the periodic table exceptions that examiners love testing.

1. Malleability (Flattening)

The property by virtue of which metals can be beaten into ultra-thin sheets with a hammer without cracking.

★ Champions: Gold (Au) & Silver (Ag) can be beaten into foils just 0.00004 mm thick (like Vark on Indian sweets)!

2. Ductility (Drawing Wires)

The ability of a material to be stretched and drawn into extremely thin, continuous wires under tensile stress.

★ Mind-Blowing Fact: A single 1-gram nugget of pure Gold can be drawn into a microscopic wire over 2 kilometers long!

3. Electrical Conductivity

Metals contain delocalised valence electrons that flow freely when an electric voltage is applied across the lattice.

★ Hierarchy: Silver (Ag) > Copper (Cu) > Aluminium (Al). Copper & Al are used practically due to affordability.

4. Thermal Conductivity

Metals rapidly conduct kinetic thermal vibrations via lattice collisions and free-electron transport.

★ Best: Silver & Copper. Cooking utensils feature copper bottoms to eliminate localized hot spots.

5. Sonority (Ringing Acoustic)

When metals are struck with a hard object, their cohesive metallic lattice vibrates without shattering, generating a prolonged ringing sound.

★ Applications: Temple bells, school bells, cymbals, guitar strings, piano wires.

6. Metallic Lustre

Freshly cut or polished metal surfaces reflect light photons cleanly due to rapid oscillations of surface valence electrons.

★ Over Time: Metals tarnish in atmospheric air because they form thin surface films of oxide, carbonate, or sulphide.

The 10 Famous Periodic Anomalies & Exceptions

100% Tested in Board & Olympiad Exams
1
Mercury (Hg) • The Liquid Metal

The ONLY metal that exists as a liquid at room temperature (25°C). It is used in glass clinical thermometers because of uniform thermal expansion.

2
Gallium (Ga) & Caesium (Cs) • Palm-Melting Metals

They have abnormally low melting points (Ga = 29.8°C, Cs = 28.4°C). If held in the palm of your hand (37°C body heat), they melt into liquid metal!

3
Sodium (Na) & Potassium (K) • Soft as Butter

Unlike standard hard metals, alkali metals have weak metallic bonding and low densities. They can be easily sliced with a dull table butter knife!

4
Lead (Pb) & Mercury (Hg) • Poor Heat Conductors

While almost all metals are exceptional conductors of heat, Lead and Mercury are uniquely poor thermal conductors among metallic elements.

5
Iodine (I₂) • The Lustrous Non-Metal

Non-metals are generally dull and non-reflective. Iodine crystals are the spectacular exception, exhibiting a dark violet metallic lustrous sheen.

6
Diamond (Carbon Allotrope) • The Hardest Natural Substance

Non-metals are typically soft or brittle. Diamond features a rigid 3D tetrahedral covalent cage, giving it extreme hardness and an astronomical melting point (> 3500°C).

7
Graphite (Carbon Allotrope) • Conducting Non-Metal

Non-metals are electrical insulators. In graphite, carbon atoms bond in hexagonal layers with 1 free unbonded electron per carbon atom, enabling electrical conduction.

8
Bromine (Br₂) • The Only Liquid Non-Metal

Non-metals are either gases (like O₂, N₂, Cl₂) or solids (like C, S, P). Bromine is the ONLY non-metallic element that is a reddish-brown liquid at room temperature.

9
Tungsten (W) • Highest Melting Point Metal

Boasts an incredible melting point of 3422°C! This makes it the sole choice for traditional glowing incandescent light bulb filaments.

10
Lithium (Li), Sodium (Na) • Float on Water

Most metals are dense and sink in water. Lithium (0.534 g/cm³) and Sodium (0.97 g/cm³) have densities lower than water (1.0 g/cm³) and float!

Reactive Kinetics

Chemical Reactions: Metals in Action

Understanding oxidation pathways, steam reactions, amphoteric dualism, and acid mechanisms.

1

Reaction of Metals with Atmospheric Oxygen (O₂)

Almost all metals combine with atmospheric oxygen to form solid metallic oxides. Because metal atoms donate electrons, metallic oxides are naturally Basic Oxides that turn red litmus paper blue.

Core Chemical Formula
2Mg (s) + O₂ (g) ➔ 2MgO (s) [Dazzling White Flame]
MgO (s) + H₂O (l) ➔ Mg(OH)₂ (aq) [Basic Alkali, Turns Red Litmus Blue]
Soluble Metal Oxides (Alkalies): Most metal oxides are insoluble in water. However, Sodium oxide (Na₂O) and Potassium oxide (K₂O) dissolve in water to produce strong soluble alkalies (NaOH and KOH).
High-Yield Board Exam Favorite

Amphoteric Oxides: The Dual Personality Oxides

Certain metal oxides show BOTH basic as well as acidic behavior! They react with acids to form salt and water, and ALSO react with strong bases to form salt and water. The two classic examples are Aluminium Oxide (Al₂O₃) and Zinc Oxide (ZnO).

Al₂O₃ behaving as a Base (Reacting with Acid):
Al₂O₃ + 6HCl ➔ 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O
Al₂O₃ behaving as an Acid (Reacting with Base):
Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH ➔ 2NaAlO₂ (Sodium Aluminate) + H₂O
ZnO behaving with Base:
ZnO + 2NaOH ➔ Na₂ZnO₂ (Sodium Zincate) + H₂O
2

Reactions of Metals with Water: 3 Distinct Tiers

Tier 1: Cold Water Violent & Exothermic

Potassium (K), Sodium (Na), Calcium (Ca)

K and Na react violently with cold water. The reaction is so exothermic that evolved H₂ gas immediately catches fire!

2Na + 2H₂O ➔ 2NaOH + H₂ ↑ + Heat
★ Why Calcium Floats: Calcium reacts less violently; the bubbles of H₂ gas stick to the surface of the calcium pieces, causing them to float!
Tier 2: Hot Water Moderate Reaction

Magnesium (Mg)

Magnesium does NOT react with cold water at all. It requires boiling hot water to react, forming magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

Mg + 2H₂O (hot) ➔ Mg(OH)₂ + H₂ ↑
★ Like Calcium, Magnesium starts floating on water because bubbles of hydrogen gas stick to its surface.
Tier 3: Steam Only High Activation Energy

Aluminium (Al), Zinc (Zn), Iron (Fe)

They do not react with cold or hot water. When steam is passed over red-hot metal, they form Metal Oxides (not hydroxides) + H₂!

3Fe (s) + 4H₂O (g) ➔ Fe₃O₄ (s) + 4H₂ ↑
★ Zero Reaction: Lead (Pb), Copper (Cu), Silver (Ag), and Gold (Au) do not react even with boiling steam.
3

Reactions of Metals with Dilute Acids

General Reaction Scheme
Metal + Dilute Acid ➔ Metal Salt + H₂ ↑ (Pop Sound Test)

Rate of reaction with dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl): Mg > Al > Zn > Fe Magnesium reacts fastest with rapid effervescence and highest temperature rise. Copper shows zero bubbles and zero reaction because it is below Hydrogen in the reactivity series.

The Nitric Acid (HNO₃) Paradox

Why doesn't HNO₃ evolve Hydrogen gas?

Nitric acid (HNO₃) is a ferocious Oxidising Agent! As soon as nascent H₂ gas is produced, HNO₃ oxidises it into water (H₂O) and reduces itself to nitrogen oxides (NO₂, NO, or N₂O).

★ The Sole Exception: Very dilute (1%) HNO₃ DOES liberate H₂ gas with Magnesium (Mg) and Manganese (Mn):
Mg + 2HNO₃ (very dilute) ➔ Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂ ↑
Royal Chemistry Solvent

Aqua Regia ("Royal Water") • 3 : 1 Ratio

A freshly prepared mixture of Concentrated Hydrochloric Acid (3 parts) and Concentrated Nitric Acid (1 part). Neither acid alone can touch noble metals, but Aqua Regia dissolves Gold (Au) and Platinum (Pt) due to nascent chlorine!

Conc. HCl : Conc. HNO₃
3 : 1

Fe

Reaction Status DISPLACEMENT OCCURS
Balanced Chemical Equation
Fe (s) + CuSO₄ (aq) ➔ FeSO₄ (aq) + Cu (s)
Observation & Scientific Reason:

Iron (Fe) lies above Copper (Cu) in the reactivity series. Iron displaces copper ions from solution: blue colour of CuSO₄ fades to pale green FeSO₄, and a reddish-brown coating of metallic copper deposits on the iron nail.

⚡

Thermite Welding Process: Extreme Single Displacement

Certain displacement reactions are so violently exothermic that the displaced metal is produced in the molten (liquid) state! The classic example is the Thermite Reaction, where aluminium powder reduces iron(III) oxide.

Fe₂O₃ (s) + 2Al (s) ➔ 2Fe (l) [Molten Iron] + Al₂O₃ (s) + Enormous Heat

The white-hot liquid iron flows directly into cracks between railway tracks or broken heavy machinery frames to weld them solid on site!

Reduction of Metal Oxides by Carbon

Why can carbon reduce Zinc, Iron, and Lead oxides, but CANNOT reduce Aluminium or Magnesium oxides?

ZnO + C ➔ Zn + CO ↑ (Carbon reduces ZnO)
Al₂O₃ + C ➔ NO REACTION (Al has higher affinity for oxygen than carbon!)
Aluminium and Magnesium are extracted by Electrolytic Reduction of their molten chlorides or oxides.
Electronegative Elements

Non-Metals Chemistry & Allotropes of Carbon

Acidic vs neutral anhydrides, electron acceptance thermodynamics, and covalent carbon allotropy.

1

Reactions of Non-Metals with Atmospheric Oxygen (O₂)

Acidic Oxides (Acid Anhydrides) Turns Blue Litmus Red

Most non-metals combine with oxygen to form covalent acidic oxides. When dissolved in water, they produce mineral acids.

S (s) + O₂ (g) ➔ SO₂ (g) [Sulphur Dioxide]
SO₂ (g) + H₂O (l) ➔ H₂SO₃ (aq) [Sulphurous Acid]
C (s) + O₂ (g) ➔ CO₂ (g) ➔ H₂CO₃ (aq) [Carbonic Acid]
Neutral Oxides Zero Litmus Effect

Certain non-metallic oxides exhibit neither acidic nor basic characteristics. They do not alter red or blue litmus papers.

• Carbon Monoxide (CO) - Toxic neutral gas
• Nitric Oxide (NO) - Neutral nitrogen oxide
• Nitrous Oxide (N₂O) - Laughing gas
• Dihydrogen Monoxide (H₂O) - Pure neutral water (pH 7)
Examiner HOTS Question

Why Do Non-Metals NEVER Displace Hydrogen Gas From Dilute Acids?

To displace Hydrogen gas (H₂) from an acid, hydrogen ions (H⁺) must gain electrons to become neutral H atoms: 2H⁺ (aq) + 2e⁻ ➔ H₂ (g) ↑ Metals are electron donors (electropositive), so they easily provide the necessary electrons. Non-metals, however, are electron acceptors (electronegative) — they cannot donate electrons to H⁺ ions! Therefore, non-metals NEVER react with dilute acids to evolve hydrogen gas.

2

Allotropes of Carbon: Same Element, Polar Opposite Behaviors

💎

Diamond

3D Rigid Tetrahedral Lattice (sp³)

Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to 4 other carbon atoms. There are ZERO free electrons.

  • Hardest naturally occurring substance
  • Extremely high melting point (> 3500°C)
  • Electrical Insulator (no mobile electrons)
  • Used in glass cutters and rock drills
✏️

Graphite

2D Hexagonal Planar Sheets (sp²)

Each carbon atom is bonded to 3 others in flat sheets. The 4th valence electron is delocalised and free to move!

  • Soft, slippery and soapy to the touch
  • Sheets slide past each other easily
  • Good Electrical Conductor
  • Used in pencil leads and solid lubricants
⚽

Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀)

Soccer Ball Cage (Geodesic Dome)

Contains 60 carbon atoms arranged in 20 interlocking hexagons and 12 pentagons, named after architect Buckminster Fuller.

  • Discrete hollow spherical molecule
  • Dark solid at room temperature
  • Semiconductor properties
  • Used in nanotechnology & drug delivery
Electrochemical Dynamics

Corrosion Kinetics & Modern Rust Prevention

Mechanism of hydrated ferric oxide, tarnish profiles across elements, and sacrificial cathodic protection.

1

The Chemistry of Iron Rusting (Fe₂O₃ · xH₂O)

Rusting of iron is an electrochemical process. Iron will NEVER rust in dry air alone or in boiled oxygen-free water alone. Rusting requires BOTH Oxygen (O₂) and Moisture (H₂O) simultaneously.

Overall Rusting Reaction
4Fe (s) + 3O₂ (g) + 2xH₂O (l) ➔ 2Fe₂O₃·xH₂O (s)
Hydrated Iron(III) Oxide • Flaky Reddish-Brown Powder

★ Why Rust is Destructive: Unlike aluminium oxide which seals the metal, iron rust is porous, brittle, and non-adherent. It flakes off continuously, exposing fresh underlying iron to oxygen and moisture until the entire iron structure crumbles away.

🥈
Silver (Ag) Black Tarnishing

Silver items turn black when exposed to air because silver reacts with traces of Hydrogen Sulphide (H₂S) in the atmosphere to form black Silver Sulphide (Ag₂S).

2Ag + H₂S ➔ Ag₂S (black) + H₂ ↑
🥉
Copper (Cu) Green Patina (Verdigris)

Copper reacts slowly with moist carbon dioxide in the air to lose its brown shine, gaining a permanent protective green coating of basic copper carbonate.

2Cu + H₂O + CO₂ + O₂ ➔ CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂ (green)
🛡️
Aluminium (Al) Self-Passivating Armor

Aluminium reacts with atmospheric oxygen to form an ultra-thin, dense, and non-porous film of Aluminium Oxide (Al₂O₃) that completely shields the interior metal from further attack!

2

6 Engineering Methods to Defeat Corrosion

1

Painting, Oiling & Greasing

Provides a physical barrier preventing air and moisture from touching iron. Applied on window grills, gates, automobile engine components, and bicycle chains.

2

Galvanisation

Sacrificial Protection

Coating iron or steel with a thin layer of molten Zinc (Zn).

Why Galvanised Iron Stays Protected Even When Scratched: Zinc is more electropositive than iron (Zn > Fe). Even if the coating cracks, Zinc sacrifices itself and oxidises preferentially, preserving the iron intact!

3

Tinning (Kalai)

Coating brass and copper cooking vessels with non-toxic molten Tin (Sn). This prevents acidic organic foods (curd, citrus, pickles) from reacting with copper to form toxic poison salts.

4

Chromium & Nickel Electroplating

Electrolytic deposition of a gleaming, hard, corrosion-resistant coating of Chromium or Nickel onto iron fixtures, bathroom taps, car bumpers, and cycle handlebars.

5

Alloying (Stainless Steel)

Iron mixed with Chromium (18%) and Nickel (8%) forms Stainless Steel. It does not rust at all, even when exposed to salt water and chemical detergents.

6

Sacrificial Cathodic Anode

Sacrificial ingots of highly reactive Magnesium (Mg) or Zinc (Zn) are bolted directly to ocean ship hulls and buried along steel underground oil pipelines to protect them from rusting.

Materials Engineering

The 10-Alloy Master Matrix & Ancient Metallurgy

Homogeneous solid solutions, composition percentages, industrial utility, and ancient Indian metallurgy.

What is an Alloy?

An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal, prepared by melting the primary metal and dissolving the other constituents into it in definite proportions, then cooling to room temperature.

1. Boost Hardness

Pure iron and pure gold are extremely soft. Adding 0.5% carbon turns iron into steel; adding copper to gold yields hard 22K jewelry.

2. Eliminate Rust

Adding chromium and nickel to iron completely stops rusting, creating shiny surgical-grade stainless steel.

3. Lower Melting Point

Pure Lead melts at 327°C and Tin at 232°C. Mixing them 50:50 creates Solder, melting at just 183°C for joining wires.

4. Lower Electrical Drift

Alloys typically have lower electrical conductivity than pure constituent metals, making them ideal high-resistance heating elements.

🏛️

Ancient Indian Metallurgy: The Rustless Iron Pillar of Delhi

Qutub Minar Complex, Mehrauli • Over 1,600 Years Old
Physical Dimensions
Height: 7.2 meters • Weight: > 6 tonnes

Constructed during the Gupta Empire (c. 400 CE) by ancient Indian blacksmiths via forge-welding wrought iron.

The Scientific Secret to Its Rust Immunity

Despite enduring 1,600+ years of Delhi monsoons, heat, and smog, it has NOT rusted! Ancient Indian metalworkers used high-phosphorus iron ore without removing slag. This catalyzed the formation of an ultra-thin, continuous, self-healing protective barrier of crystalline iron hydrogen phosphate hydrate (α-FeOOH / misawite), completely blocking oxygen and water from touching the metal!

Activity 3.14 Simulator

The 3-Test-Tubes Rusting Investigation

Click any tube to inspect environmental conditions and verify why rusting requires BOTH air and moisture.

Tube A: Air + Tap Water
Outcome: RUSTS HEAVILY
Tube B: Boiled Water + Oil Layer
Outcome: ZERO RUST (Clean & Shiny)

Outcome: ZERO RUST (Clean & Shiny)
Tube A Diagnostics: Air + Normal Tap Water Rusting Occurs

The nails are exposed to both atmospheric oxygen dissolved in water and moisture from the water itself. After a few days, an extensive reddish-brown flaky deposit of hydrated ferric oxide (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O) covers the iron nails.

Activity 3.1 & 3.2 Mechanical Test

Malleability & Hardness of Elements

Procedure: Place an iron nail, a piece of aluminium wire, a lump of coal, and pencil lead on an iron anvil and strike repeatedly with a heavy hammer.

• Iron & Aluminium: Flatten into thin sheets without breaking (Malleable).
• Coal & Pencil Lead: Shatter into tiny fragments & powder (Brittle Non-Metals).
Activity 3.6 Circuit Test

Electrical Conductivity Test

Procedure: Set up an electrical circuit with a 6V battery, bulb, switch, and two clip terminals A and B. Insert various samples between the clips.

• Copper / Aluminium / Iron: Bulb glows brightly (Conductors).
• Sulphur / Coal piece: Bulb does not glow (Insulators).
• Pencil Lead (Graphite): Bulb glows! (Graphite is an exceptional conducting non-metal).
Activity 3.8 (Part 1) Combustion

Burning Magnesium Ribbon in Air

Procedure: Clean a magnesium ribbon with sandpaper and burn it in a Bunsen burner flame using tongs. Collect white ash, dissolve in water, and test with litmus.

• Burns with dazzling white flame producing white powder MgO.
• MgO + H₂O ➔ Mg(OH)₂ (turns red litmus blue ➔ Basic Oxide).
Activity 3.8 (Part 2) Acid Anhydride

Burning Sulphur in Deflagrating Spoon

Procedure: Heat sulphur powder in a deflagrating spoon inside a gas jar covered with a lid. Add water, shake, and test with red and blue litmus paper.

• Sulphur burns with a blue flame producing pungent gas SO₂.
• SO₂ + H₂O ➔ H₂SO₃ (turns blue litmus red ➔ Acidic Oxide).
Activity 3.10 Water Reactivity

Metals Reaction with Cold, Hot & Steam

Procedure: Drop metal samples into beakers of cold water, hot water, and pass steam over heated metals in a glass combustion tube.

• Na / K: Reacts violently with cold water, catches fire.
• Ca: Reacts calmly, floats due to H₂ bubbles.
• Mg: Reacts only with hot boiling water.
• Al / Fe / Zn: React only with dry steam, forming metal oxides.
Activity 3.11 Pop Sound Test

Metal Reactions with Dilute Hydrochloric Acid

Procedure: Add dilute HCl to test tubes containing Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, and Cu. Bring a burning candle splinter near the mouth of the test tube.

• Mg, Al, Zn, Fe produce gas that extinguishes flame with a sharp 'POP' sound (Hydrogen gas confirmation).
• Copper shows zero bubbles and zero reaction.

Q1 • Short Answer True or False with Scientific Justification
medium 3 Marks
State with reason(s) whether True [T] or False [F]: (i) Aluminium and copper are examples of non-metals used for making utensils and statues [ ] (ii) Metals form oxides when combined with oxygen, the solution of which turns blue litmus paper to red [ ] (iii) Oxygen is a non-metal essential for respiration [ ] (iv) Copper vessels are used for boiling water because they are good conductors of electricity [ ]
Model Textbook Answer
(i) False [F]: Aluminium and copper are metals, not non-metals. They possess metallic lustre, malleability, and high thermal conductivity.
(ii) False [F]: Metallic oxides are basic in nature; their aqueous solutions turn red litmus paper to blue, not blue to red.
(iii) True [T]: Oxygen is a gaseous non-metal that is essential for cellular respiration in living aerobic organisms.
(iv) False [F]: Copper vessels are used for boiling water because copper is an excellent conductor of heat (thermal conductivity), not electricity.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Scientific understanding requires distinguishing thermal conductivity from electrical conductivity, and recognizing basic metal oxides.
Q2 • Short Answer Suitability of Metals for Jewellery
easy 2 Marks
Why are only a few metals suitable for making jewellery?
Model Textbook Answer
Only a few metals—such as gold, silver, and platinum—are used for jewellery because:
1. They are highly unreactive noble metals that do not corrode, tarnish, or react with air, water, or sweat.
2. They possess permanent, lustrous shine.
3. They are exceptionally malleable and ductile, allowing intricate shaping into delicate ornamental designs.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Resistance to chemical corrosion and high ductility make noble metals uniquely suited for jewellery.
Q3 • Short Answer Comparison of Oxide Nature
medium 2 Marks
What happens when oxygen reacts with magnesium and sulphur? What are the differences in the nature of products formed?
Model Textbook Answer
- Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide (MgO):
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. When dissolved in water, it forms Mg(OH)₂, which is BASIC in nature and turns red litmus paper blue.
- Sulphur reacts with oxygen to form sulphur dioxide (SO₂):
S + O₂ → SO₂. When dissolved in water, it forms sulphurous acid (H₂SO₃), which is ACIDIC in nature and turns blue litmus paper red.
Difference: Magnesium oxide is a basic metallic oxide, whereas sulphur dioxide is an acidic non-metallic oxide.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Metals produce basic oxides; non-metals produce acidic oxides.
Q4 • Short Answer Magnesium Combustion Flowchart
medium 3 Marks
Complete the following flow chart: (?) + Air + Heat → Ash → + Water → (?) Add blue and red litmus solution separately: - Change in blue litmus solution: (?) - Change in red litmus solution: Blue
Model Textbook Answer
1. Starting material (?): Magnesium ribbon [Mg]
2. Burning reaction: 2Mg + O₂ --Heat--> 2MgO (Ash)
3. Dissolving in water: MgO + H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ (Solution of magnesium hydroxide)
4. Change in blue litmus solution: No change (remains blue)
5. Change in red litmus solution: Turns Blue (confirms basic nature of magnesium hydroxide).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Magnesium burning yields basic MgO; MgO in water forms alkaline Mg(OH)₂.
Q5 • Short Answer Selection of Cookware Materials
medium 2 Marks
You are provided with the following materials: Iron, copper, sulphur, coal, plastic, wood, cardboard. Discuss which material would be your choice to make a pan suitable for boiling water and why?
Model Textbook Answer
Copper (or Iron) would be the choice for making the pan body.
Why: Copper is a metal with very high thermal conductivity, high melting point, and excellent mechanical strength, allowing rapid, uniform heating without melting or burning.
Materials like sulphur and coal are brittle non-metals that would burn or break; wood and cardboard would catch fire; and plastic would melt at boiling temperatures.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Cookware demands high thermal conductivity and thermal stability.
Q6 • Short Answer Rusting Environment Comparison
medium 2 Marks
You are provided with three iron nails, each dipped in oil, water and vinegar. Which iron nail will not rust, and why?
Model Textbook Answer
The iron nail dipped in oil will not rust.
Why: Rusting requires both moisture (water) and oxygen (air). The layer of oil forms an impenetrable barrier that cuts off exposure to atmospheric oxygen and water.
- The nail in water rusts because both water and dissolved oxygen are present.
- The nail in vinegar reacts vigorously with acetic acid, corroding rapidly.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Oil excludes both air and water, preventing electrochemical rust formation.
Q7 • Short Answer Properties Determining Everyday Uses
medium 3 Marks
How do the different properties of metals and non-metals determine their uses in everyday life?
Model Textbook Answer
1. Metals:
- High electrical conductivity and ductility determine copper and aluminium's use in electric transmission wires.
- High thermal conductivity and malleability determine aluminium and copper's use in cooking utensils.
- Lustre and non-corrosive noble nature determine gold and silver's use in jewellery.
2. Non-metals:
- High tensile strength and hardness determine diamond's use in cutting glass and rock drill bits.
- Electrical conductivity determines graphite's use as battery electrodes.
- Disinfecting properties determine chlorine's use in water purification.
- Essential biochemical reactivity determines oxygen's use in medical life support.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Specific physical and chemical properties dictate technological suitability.
Q8 • Short Answer Sulphur Coating vs Galvanization Justification
medium 2 Marks
One of the methods of protecting iron from getting rusted is to put a thin coating of zinc metal over it. Since sulphur does not react with water, can it be used for this purpose? Justify your answer.
Model Textbook Answer
No, sulphur cannot be used to protect iron from rusting.
Justification:
1. Sulphur is a brittle non-metal that lacks malleability and ductility; it cannot form a flexible, adherent, uniform metallic coating on iron and would easily crumble or peel off.
2. In the presence of air, sulphur slowly oxidises to sulphur dioxide (SO₂), which reacts with moisture to form sulphurous/sulphuric acid, accelerating the corrosion of iron.
3. Zinc is malleable, strongly adheres to iron, and provides sacrificial cathodic protection.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Coatings must be adherent, durable, and chemically stable against atmospheric oxidation.
Q9 • Short Answer Thermal Softening of Iron in Blacksmithing
easy 2 Marks
An ironsmith heats iron before making tools. Why is heating necessary in this process?
Model Textbook Answer
An ironsmith heats iron to red hot because iron becomes much softer and highly malleable at elevated temperatures. Heating weakens the interatomic metallic bonds, allowing the iron to be easily hammered, bent, flattened, and shaped into desired tools without fracturing or cracking.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Thermal activation increases metal ductility and malleability, enabling plastic deformation.
Q10 • Short Answer Metal Displacement Reactions
medium 2 Marks
In four test tubes, some metals are in contact with salt solutions: (A) FeSO₄ + Cu (B) ZnSO₄ + Fe (C) CuSO₄ + Zn (D) ZnSO₄ + Cu After the experiment, in which of the test tubes does the solution become colourless and a powdery red mass is deposited at the bottom of the test tube?
Model Textbook Answer
In test tube (C), containing CuSO₄ and Zn.
Reaction: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) [Blue] → ZnSO₄(aq) [Colourless] + Cu(s) [Reddish-brown powder].
Examiner & Concept Tip: Zinc is more reactive than copper in the activity series, so it displaces copper from copper sulphate solution, forming colourless zinc sulphate and precipitating metallic copper powder. In tubes A, B, and D, no displacement occurs.
Q11 • Short Answer Reactivity of Silver with Copper Sulphate
easy 2 Marks
A silver spoon is kept immersed in an aqueous solution of copper sulphate. What change will take place?
Model Textbook Answer
No change will take place. The silver spoon will remain unaffected, and the blue colour of the copper sulphate solution will not fade.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Silver (Ag) lies below copper (Cu) in the reactivity series and is less reactive than copper; hence, silver cannot displace copper from copper sulphate solution.
Q12 • Short Answer Corrosion via Displacement in Iron Containers
medium 2 Marks
A solution of copper sulphate was stored in an iron container. After a few days, some holes were seen in the iron container. Explain the observation.
Model Textbook Answer
Iron is more reactive than copper and displaces copper from copper sulphate solution:
Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)
As iron from the container walls continuously dissolves to form ferrous sulphate, the metal is eaten away, creating holes in the container.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Displacement reactions between storage metal and aqueous metal salts can cause severe container failure.
Q13 • Short Answer Reactions with Dilute Acids
easy 2 Marks
What happens when samples of metals and non-metals are mixed with acids?
Model Textbook Answer
- Metals (that lie above hydrogen in the reactivity series) react with dilute acids to produce a metal salt and evolve hydrogen gas (H₂), which burns with a characteristic pop sound.
- Non-metals generally do not react with dilute acids because they cannot donate electrons to reduce H⁺ ions into hydrogen gas.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Acid displacement requires electron transfer: M → Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻; 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂↑.
Q14 • Short Answer Chemical Comparison of Metals and Non-metals
medium 3 Marks
Compare metals and non-metals on the basis of chemical properties.
Model Textbook Answer
1. Reaction with oxygen: Metals form basic oxides (e.g., Na₂O, MgO); Non-metals form acidic or neutral oxides (e.g., SO₂, CO₂; CO, H₂O).
2. Reaction with water: Reactive metals displace hydrogen from water/steam; Non-metals do not react with water.
3. Reaction with acids: Metals above hydrogen displace H₂ from dilute acids; Non-metals do not react with dilute acids.
4. Displacement in salt solutions: More reactive metals displace less reactive metals; Non-metals do not show this type of metallic displacement.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Metals are electropositive electron donors; non-metals are electronegative electron acceptors.
Q15 • Short Answer Constituent Elements in Bases and Acids
medium 3 Marks
Name the metals present in the bases and non-metals present in the acids listed below: (i) Slaked lime (ii) Magnesium hydroxide (iii) Caustic soda (iv) Zinc hydroxide (v) Sulphuric acid (vi) Nitric acid (vii) Phosphoric acid (viii) Carbonic acid
Model Textbook Answer
Metals in bases:
(i) Slaked lime [Ca(OH)₂]: Calcium
(ii) Magnesium hydroxide [Mg(OH)₂]: Magnesium
(iii) Caustic soda [NaOH]: Sodium
(iv) Zinc hydroxide [Zn(OH)₂]: Zinc
Non-metals in acids:
(v) Sulphuric acid [H₂SO₄]: Sulphur, Oxygen (and Hydrogen)
(vi) Nitric acid [HNO₃]: Nitrogen, Oxygen (and Hydrogen)
(vii) Phosphoric acid [H₃PO₄]: Phosphorus, Oxygen (and Hydrogen)
(viii) Carbonic acid [H₂CO₃]: Carbon, Oxygen (and Hydrogen)
Examiner & Concept Tip: Bases are metallic hydroxides; oxoacids contain non-metallic central atoms.
Q16 • Short Answer Feasibility of Displacement Reactions
medium 2 Marks
Which of the following reactions cannot take place? Justify your answer. (i) Iron + Zinc sulphate → Iron sulphate + Zinc (ii) Copper + Silver nitrate → Copper nitrate + Silver (iii) Zinc + Iron sulphate → Zinc sulphate + Iron (iv) Iron + Copper sulphate → Iron sulphate + Copper
Model Textbook Answer
Reaction (i) cannot take place: Iron + Zinc sulphate → No reaction.
Justification: In the reactivity series, iron is less reactive than zinc. A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive metal from its salt solution. In reactions (ii), (iii), and (iv), the free metal is more reactive than the metal in solution, so those reactions proceed readily.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Reactivity order: Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag.
Q17 • Short Answer Balancing Combustion Reactions
medium 3 Marks
Complete the following chemical reactions: (i) Sulphur + Oxygen → (ii) Phosphorus + Oxygen → (iii) Carbon + Oxygen → (iv) Zinc + Oxygen → (v) Sodium + Oxygen →
Model Textbook Answer
(i) 2S + 3O₂ → 2SO₃ (or S + O₂ → SO₂)
(ii) 4P + 5O₂ → 2P₂O₅
(iii) 2C + O₂ → 2CO (or C + O₂ → CO₂)
(iv) 2Zn + O₂ → 2ZnO
(v) 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O
Examiner & Concept Tip: Non-metals form non-metallic oxides; metals form basic metallic oxides.
Q18 • Short Answer Metal Reactions with Water and Steam
medium 3 Marks
Explain reactions of sodium, magnesium and iron with water.
Model Textbook Answer
(i) Sodium: Reacts violently with cold water to form sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas, generating so much heat that hydrogen catches fire:
2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g)↑ + Heat
(ii) Magnesium: Does not react with cold water; reacts slowly with hot/boiling water to produce magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen gas:
Mg(s) + 2H₂O(l) --Hot water--> Mg(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g)↑
(With steam: Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂↑)
(iii) Iron: Does not react with cold or hot water; reacts only when red-hot with steam to form magnetic iron oxide and hydrogen gas:
3Fe(s) + 4H₂O(g) --Red hot--> Fe₃O₄(s) + 4H₂(g)↑
Examiner & Concept Tip: The vigorousness of water reactions mirrors position in the activity series: Na > Mg > Fe.
Q19 • Short Answer Alloys and Aircraft Construction
medium 2 Marks
(i) What is an alloy? (ii) A light and strong alloy is required for making bodies of aircrafts; what should be its constituents?
Model Textbook Answer
(i) An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal, prepared by fusing the components in the molten state.
(ii) The alloy used for aircraft bodies is Duralumin. Its constituents are Aluminium (Al, 95%), Copper (Cu, 4%), Manganese (Mn, 0.5%), and Magnesium (Mg, 0.5%). It is lightweight, exceptionally strong, and corrosion-resistant.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Pure aluminium is lightweight but lacks tensile strength; alloying with copper and magnesium creates high strength-to-weight ratio.
Q20 • Short Answer Galvanized and Passive Iron
medium 2 Marks
Define the terms: galvanized iron and passive iron.
Model Textbook Answer
1. Galvanized Iron: Iron coated with a thin protective layer of zinc metal (either by dipping in molten zinc or electroplating) to prevent rusting.
2. Passive Iron: When iron is treated with concentrated nitric acid (HNO₃), a non-porous, protective insoluble oxide film is formed on its surface, which renders the iron chemically inactive (inert) and stops further corrosion. Iron in this state is called passive iron.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Galvanizing provides sacrificial barrier protection; passivity results from surface oxide passivation.
Q21 • Short Answer Identification of Aluminium and its Oxide
easy 2 Marks
Metal M occurs in earth's crust as its oxide M₂O₃. An alloy of this metal is used in making aircrafts. Name the metal M and its oxide.
Model Textbook Answer
Metal M is Aluminium (Al). Its oxide is Aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃), commonly found as the mineral bauxite.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Aluminium forms Al₂O₃ and its alloy duralumin is used in aircraft manufacture.
Q22 • Short Answer Metal Resources and Recycling
easy 2 Marks
Are metals renewable resources? If not, can they be recycled?
Model Textbook Answer
No, metals are non-renewable resources because they are extracted from finite mineral ores in the Earth's crust that took millions of years to form. However, metals can be recycled repeatedly by remelting and refabricating without losing their chemical or physical properties (e.g., recycling aluminium, copper, steel, and gold).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Recycling metals preserves scarce ores and saves up to 95% processing energy.
Q23 • Short Answer Malleability Definition and Examples
easy 1 Marks
What is malleability? Name two most malleable metals.
Model Textbook Answer
Malleability is the physical property of metals that allows them to be hammered or rolled into very thin sheets without cracking or breaking. Gold (Au) and Silver (Ag) are the two most malleable metals.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Gold can be beaten into leaves less than 0.0001 mm thick.
Q24 • Short Answer Sodium Reaction with Water Activity
medium 3 Marks
Explain the reaction of sodium and water with the help of an activity.
Model Textbook Answer
Activity Protocol:
1. Fill a glass beaker half with water.
2. Cut a small piece of sodium metal using a dry knife and dry it between folds of filter paper.
3. Wrap the sodium piece in a small tuft of cotton and gently drop it into the water using tongs.
4. Observation: The sodium darts rapidly on the water surface with a hissing sound, melts into a shiny silvery ball, catches fire, and burns with a golden-yellow flame. The beaker becomes distinctly hot.
5. Test: Dip red litmus paper into the resulting solution; the red litmus paper turns BLUE.
Chemical Equation:
2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g)↑ + Heat
Conclusion: Sodium is an extremely reactive metal that reacts vigorously and exothermically with cold water, evolving hydrogen gas and forming basic sodium hydroxide.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Exothermic heat of reaction ignites the evolved hydrogen gas.
Q25 • Short Answer Metalloids Definition
easy 1 Marks
What are the elements which show properties of both metals and non-metals called?
Model Textbook Answer
Metalloids (or semimetals, e.g., silicon, germanium, arsenic).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Elements with intermediate physical and chemical characteristics are classified as metalloids.
Q26 • Short Answer Displacement Reaction
easy 1 Marks
Name the reaction in which more reactive metal displaces less reactive metal from its salt solution.
Model Textbook Answer
Displacement reaction (or Single displacement reaction).
Examiner & Concept Tip: A more electropositive metal donates electrons to displace a less reactive metal cation from solution.
Q27 • Short Answer Galvanization Definition
easy 1 Marks
What is galvanization?
Model Textbook Answer
Galvanization is the metallurgical process of coating iron or steel articles with a thin protective layer of zinc metal to prevent rusting.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Zinc acts as a physical barrier and offers sacrificial cathodic protection.
Q28 • Short Answer Cookware Metals
easy 1 Marks
Why aluminium and copper metals are used for making utensils?
Model Textbook Answer
Because aluminium and copper are excellent conductors of heat, have high melting points, and are easily shaped due to high malleability.
Examiner & Concept Tip: High thermal conductivity ensures uniform cooking without scorching.
Q29 • Short Answer Chemical Name of Rust
easy 1 Marks
What is rust chemically known as?
Model Textbook Answer
Hydrated iron(III) oxide [Fe₂O₃·xH₂O].
Examiner & Concept Tip: Rust is formed by the electrochemical oxidation of iron in the presence of water and oxygen.
Q30 • Short Answer Litmus on Metal Oxides
easy 1 Marks
What happens when a solution of metal oxide is tested with (i) blue litmus and (ii) red litmus?
Model Textbook Answer
(i) Blue litmus shows no change in colour.
(ii) Red litmus paper turns blue (confirming basic nature).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Metal oxides dissolve in water to produce alkaline hydroxides that turn red litmus blue.
Q31 • Short Answer Alloys of Copper
easy 1 Marks
Name the alloy of copper which is used in making utensils and vessels.
Model Textbook Answer
Brass (alloy of copper and zinc) or Bronze (alloy of copper and tin).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Brass is harder and more corrosion-resistant than pure copper, making it ideal for vessels.
Q32 • Short Answer Physical Properties of Metals
easy 1 Marks
List four physical properties of metals.
Model Textbook Answer
1. Malleability (can be hammered into sheets)
2. Ductility (can be drawn into wires)
3. High thermal and electrical conductivity
4. Metallic lustre (shiny surface).
Examiner & Concept Tip: These properties originate from delocalized metallic bonding.
Q33 • Short Answer Solder Alloy
easy 1 Marks
Name the alloy of lead used in joining metals for electrical work.
Model Textbook Answer
Solder (an alloy of lead, Pb, and tin, Sn).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Solder has a low melting point (~180–200°C), making it ideal for joining electrical circuits.
Q34 • Short Answer Electrical Conductivity of Metals
easy 1 Marks
Why are metals good conductors of electricity?
Model Textbook Answer
Because metals possess a sea of free, mobile valence electrons that can drift easily through the metallic lattice under an applied electric field.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Delocalized electron mobility is responsible for electrical conduction.
Q35 • Short Answer Most Malleable Metals
easy 1 Marks
Name two most malleable metals.
Model Textbook Answer
Gold (Au) and Silver (Ag).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Gold can be beaten into sheets less than 0.0001 mm thick without cracking.
Q36 • Short Answer Decreasing Reactivity Order
medium 1 Marks
Arrange Ca, Zn, Fe, Au, Ag and Cu in order of decreasing reactivity.
Model Textbook Answer
Ca > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Decreasing activity series: Calcium > Zinc > Iron > Copper > Silver > Gold.
Q37 • Short Answer Bottom of Reactivity Series
easy 1 Marks
What is the most common property of the metals lying at the bottom of the reactivity series?
Model Textbook Answer
They are chemically unreactive, noble, and resist oxidation or corrosion, occurring in the free (native) state in nature.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Noble metals (Au, Pt, Ag) have very high positive reduction potentials.
Q38 • Short Answer Amalgam Definition
easy 1 Marks
What is an amalgam?
Model Textbook Answer
An amalgam is an alloy in which one of the constituent metals is liquid mercury (Hg).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Examples include sodium amalgam (reducing agent) and dental silver amalgam.
Q39 • Short Answer Graphite Resemblance to Metals
easy 1 Marks
In what respect does graphite resemble a metal?
Model Textbook Answer
Graphite resembles a metal in that it is an excellent conductor of electricity and possesses a greyish metallic lustre.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Free pi electrons in graphite's planar hexagonal graphene sheets conduct electrical current.
Q40 • Short Answer Definitions of Metal Properties
easy 2 Marks
Complete the given table about properties of metals: (a) Can be beaten into thin sheets (b) Can be pulled into wires (c) Gives a ringing sound when hit (d) Has a shiny appearance
Model Textbook Answer
(a) Malleability
(b) Ductility
(c) Sonority (or Sonorous nature)
(d) Metallic Lustre
Examiner & Concept Tip: Standard definitions of foundational physical properties of metals.
Q41 • Short Answer Elemental Classification from List
medium 3 Marks
For the list of elements: mercury, carbon, hydrogen, tin, sulphur, bromine, magnesium, silicon: (a) Which of the elements are solids? (b) Which of the elements are liquids? (c) Which of the elements are gases? (d) Which of the elements are metals? (e) Which of the elements are non-metals? (f) Which of the following elements are sonorous?
Model Textbook Answer
(a) Solids: Carbon, tin, sulphur, magnesium, silicon
(b) Liquids: Mercury, bromine
(c) Gases: Hydrogen
(d) Metals: Mercury, tin, magnesium
(e) Non-metals: Carbon, hydrogen, sulphur, bromine (and silicon is metalloid/non-metal)
(f) Sonorous: Tin and magnesium (metals).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Systematic categorization by state of matter and metallic character.
Q42 • Short Answer Combustion of Magnesium
easy 2 Marks
What happens when a magnesium ribbon is heated in presence of air?
Model Textbook Answer
When magnesium ribbon is heated in air, it ignites and burns vigorously with a dazzling white light to form a white powdery substance called magnesium oxide:
2Mg(s) + O₂(g) --Heat--> 2MgO(s)
Examiner & Concept Tip: Magnesium readily reacts exothermically with atmospheric oxygen to form basic magnesium oxide.
Q43 • Short Answer Everyday Uses of Metals
easy 2 Marks
List few important uses of metals.
Model Textbook Answer
1. Copper and aluminium are used in making electric wires and cooking utensils.
2. Iron is used in constructing bridges, railway tracks, buildings, and machinery.
3. Gold and silver are used for jewellery, decorative coins, and microelectronics.
4. Zinc is used for galvanizing iron sheets to prevent rusting.
5. Mercury is used in thermometers and barometers.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Versatile physical and chemical attributes make metals indispensable to modern infrastructure.
Q44 • Short Answer Displacement Observations
medium 2 Marks
What will happen if you drop: (a) some pieces of magnesium ribbon into blue copper sulphate solution? (b) some tin pieces into green ferrous sulphate solution?
Model Textbook Answer
(a) Magnesium is much more reactive than copper; it displaces copper rapidly. The blue colour of copper sulphate fades to colourless, and reddish-brown copper metal precipitates:
Mg(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)
(b) Tin is less reactive than iron (Sn < Fe in reactivity series); therefore, no displacement reaction occurs and the green ferrous sulphate solution remains unchanged.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Displacement only takes place when the added elemental metal is more reactive than the metal in solution.
Q45 • Short Answer Jewellery Metals
easy 2 Marks
Gold, platinum and silver are used to make jewellery. Give reasons.
Model Textbook Answer
1. They possess brilliant, lustrous shine that can be polished.
2. They are noble metals that do not react with atmospheric oxygen, moisture, or sweat, resisting corrosion and tarnishing.
3. They are highly malleable and ductile, allowing goldsmiths to craft intricate ornamental patterns.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Aesthetic brilliance combined with chemical inertness preserves jewellery value.
Q46 • Short Answer Atmospheric Tarnishing
easy 2 Marks
Why do some metals acquire a dull appearance on exposure to air for a long time?
Model Textbook Answer
When metals are exposed to moist air, they react slowly with atmospheric oxygen, moisture, carbon dioxide, or hydrogen sulphide, forming a thin, dull surface coating of oxide, carbonate, or sulphide (corrosion). This film scatters light and masks the underlying metallic lustre.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Surface chemical oxidation creates opaque mineral compounds that dull the metal shine.
Q47 • Short Answer Electronic Basis of Conductivity
medium 2 Marks
Give reasons why metals are good conductors, whereas non-metals are bad conductors of electricity.
Model Textbook Answer
Metals have loosely bound valence electrons that are free to move throughout the metallic crystal lattice ('free electron sea'), allowing electric charge to flow freely. Non-metals hold their valence electrons tightly in covalent bonds or localized atomic orbitals; having no free mobile electrons, they cannot conduct electricity (with graphite being the sole exception).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Mobile charge carriers are required for electrical conduction.
Q48 • Short Answer Lightweight Metals
easy 2 Marks
Why are some metals light in weight? Give examples of few light metals.
Model Textbook Answer
Some metals have low atomic masses and relatively large atomic radii with open crystal structures, resulting in low mass per unit volume (low density). Examples of light metals include:
1. Lithium (density 0.53 g/cm³, floats on water)
2. Sodium (density 0.97 g/cm³)
3. Potassium (density 0.86 g/cm³)
4. Magnesium (density 1.74 g/cm³)
5. Aluminium (density 2.70 g/cm³).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Alkali and light alkaline earth metals have low densities compared to heavy transition metals.
Q49 • Short Answer Water Reactivity Comparison
medium 2 Marks
Arrange the metals Na, Ca and Mg in decreasing order of reactivity on the basis of reaction with water.
Model Textbook Answer
Decreasing order: Na > Ca > Mg.
Justification: Sodium reacts violently with cold water, catching fire. Calcium reacts vigorously with cold water without catching fire. Magnesium does not react with cold water at all, reacting only with hot or boiling water.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Activation energy for water reduction increases down this sequence.
Q50 • Short Answer Brass vs Bronze Composition
easy 2 Marks
How do alloys, brass and bronze differ in composition?
Model Textbook Answer
- Brass is an alloy of Copper (Cu) and Zinc (Zn).
- Bronze is an alloy of Copper (Cu) and Tin (Sn).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Brass pairs copper with zinc; bronze pairs copper with tin.
Q51 • Short Answer Anomalous Inertness of Aluminium
medium 2 Marks
Aluminium metal is not as reactive as expected. Why?
Model Textbook Answer
Although aluminium is high in the reactivity series, upon exposure to air it instantly forms a thin, tough, invisible, non-porous surface coating of aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃). This protective oxide film strongly adheres to the metal and shields the underlying aluminium from reacting with air, water, or mild acids.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Surface passivation by Al₂O₃ provides exceptional chemical durability.
Q52 • Short Answer Hydrogen Evolution from HCl
easy 2 Marks
Which of the following metals will give hydrogen with dilute hydrochloric acid? Fe, Cu, Mg
Model Textbook Answer
Iron (Fe) and Magnesium (Mg) will liberate hydrogen gas.
Copper (Cu) will not.
Chemical Equations:
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)↑
Fe(s) + 2HCl(aq) → FeCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)↑
Cu(s) + HCl(aq) → No reaction (Cu lies below hydrogen).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Only metals with a negative reduction potential relative to hydrogen can displace H₂.
Q53 • Short Answer Aluminium and Copper Displacement Feasibility
medium 2 Marks
Explain why aluminium metal can displace copper from copper sulphate solution but copper cannot displace aluminium from aluminium sulphate solution?
Model Textbook Answer
In the electrochemical reactivity series, aluminium lies significantly higher than copper (Al > Cu), indicating that aluminium has a much greater tendency to lose electrons and oxidise. Therefore, aluminium can reduce Cu²⁺ ions to metallic copper:
2Al(s) + 3CuSO₄(aq) → Al₂(SO₄)₃(aq) + 3Cu(s)
Conversely, copper is far less reactive and cannot donate electrons to displace aluminium from its stable aqueous salt.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Displacement reactions are irreversible when the free element has lower oxidation potential.
Q54 • Short Answer Hammering Iron vs Wood
easy 2 Marks
Compare the changes taking place in an iron piece and a wood log on beating with a hammer.
Model Textbook Answer
- Iron piece: Iron is a malleable metal. On beating with a hammer, it flattens and expands into a thin sheet without breaking.
- Wood log: Wood is an organic non-metallic cellular material. On hammering, it does not flatten into sheets; it splinters, cracks, or fractures into rough pieces.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Metallic bonding permits atomic layers to slide without fracture; non-metallic structures cleave.
Q55 • Long Answer Identification of Metal from Properties Table
hard 5 Marks
Two properties of four substances A, B, C and D are given in the table: - Substance A: Melting point 1100°C; Electrical conductivity (Solid: Good, Molten: Good) - Substance B: Melting point 1234°C; Electrical conductivity (Solid: Poor, Molten: Good) - Substance C: Melting point 2027°C; Electrical conductivity (Solid: Poor, Molten: Poor) - Substance D: Melting point 15°C; Electrical conductivity (Solid: Poor, Molten: Poor) Which of these substances is most likely a metal and why?
Model Textbook Answer
Substance A is most likely a metal.
Why:
1. Metals are characterized by high melting points due to strong metallic bonds, and Substance A has a high melting point of 1100°C.
2. Uniquely, metals conduct electricity exceptionally well in BOTH the solid state and the molten state because of the presence of free, mobile delocalized valence electrons throughout the lattice.
- Substance B behaves as an ionic compound (insulator as solid, conductor when molten due to free ions).
- Substance C is a covalent network solid (like quartz/silicon carbide).
- Substance D is a simple molecular non-metal substance with low melting point.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Conduction in the solid state is the defining physical criterion of metallic bonding.
Q56 • Long Answer Identification of Non-metals from Uses
medium 5 Marks
Identify the non-metals on the basis of their uses: (i) Non-metal essential for all living beings for survival. (ii) Non-metal used in fertilizers to enhance growth of plants. (iii) Non-metal used in water purification process. (iv) Non-metal used in purple coloured solution which is applied on wounds as an antiseptic. (v) Non-metal used in crackers and fireworks.
Model Textbook Answer
(i) Oxygen (O₂) - required for aerobic cellular respiration.
(ii) Nitrogen (N₂) [or Phosphorus] - essential plant macronutrient in fertilizers.
(iii) Chlorine (Cl₂) - disinfectant that kills pathogenic bacteria in drinking water.
(iv) Iodine (I₂) - formulated as tincture of iodine (antiseptic for cuts).
(v) Sulphur (S) [or Phosphorus] - combustible ingredient in gunpowder and fireworks.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Non-metals play crucial biochemical, industrial, and medical roles.
Q57 • Long Answer Harmful vs Beneficial Corrosion
medium 5 Marks
What are the harmful effects of corrosion? Mention a type of corrosion which is helpful to the metal.
Model Textbook Answer
1. Harmful Effects of Corrosion:
(a) Weakens Structural Integrity: Corrosion converts strong metals into fragile, porous compounds. It severely damages railway bridges, ships, pipelines, railings, and automobile bodies.
(b) Huge Economic Losses: Billions of dollars are spent annually worldwide to replace corroded structural steel and machinery.
(c) Safety Hazards: Corroded gas or chemical pipelines can burst, causing lethal leaks and industrial catastrophes.
2. Helpful Corrosion:
- The corrosion of Aluminium is beneficial to the metal. When aluminium is exposed to air, it spontaneously oxidises to form a micro-thin, tough, continuous, non-porous layer of aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) on its surface. Unlike iron rust, this oxide layer does not flake off; it strongly adheres to the metal surface, completely sealing it off and protecting the underlying aluminium from any further atmospheric or chemical corrosion.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Iron rust is porous and destructive; aluminium oxide passivates and shields.
Q58 • Long Answer Displacement Reaction of Iron Knife in CuSO₄
hard 5 Marks
Define displacement reaction. An iron knife kept in blue copper sulphate solution turns the blue solution into light green. Explain.
Model Textbook Answer
1. Definition: A chemical reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its aqueous salt solution is called a displacement reaction.
2. Explanation:
- In the metal reactivity series, Iron (Fe) is placed above Copper (Cu) and is therefore more electropositive and chemically reactive than copper.
- When an iron knife is placed in an aqueous solution of blue copper sulphate (CuSO₄), iron atoms lose electrons to form ferrous ions (Fe²⁺), entering the solution:
Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) [Blue] → FeSO₄(aq) [Light Green] + Cu(s) [Reddish-brown]
- The displaced copper ions (Cu²⁺) gain electrons and precipitate out as a reddish-brown layer of elemental copper on the surface of the iron knife.
- The original blue color of the solution (due to Cu²⁺ ions) gradually fades and transforms into light green due to the accumulation of newly formed ferrous sulphate (FeSO₄) in solution.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Redox displacement: Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s).
Q59 • Long Answer Activity Demonstrating Acidic Non-metal Oxide
medium 5 Marks
With a suitable activity show that sulphur burns in air to form a compound which is acidic in nature.
Model Textbook Answer
Experimental Activity:
1. Materials Required: Powdered sulphur, deflagrating spoon, burner, gas jar with lid, water, and blue litmus paper.
2. Procedure:
- Place a small amount of powdered sulphur in a deflagrating spoon and heat it over a burner flame until it begins to burn with a pale blue flame.
- Immediately lower the burning spoon into a glass jar and cover it with a glass lid to trap the gas produced.
- After the sulphur stops burning, remove the spoon, quickly pour 10-15 mL of water into the jar, replace the lid, and shake vigorously to dissolve the gas.
3. Testing:
- Dip a strip of moist blue litmus paper into the resulting solution.
4. Observation:
- The blue litmus paper immediately turns RED.
5. Chemical Equations:
- Burning of sulphur: S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g) [Sulphur dioxide gas]
- Dissolving in water: SO₂(g) + H₂O(l) → H₂SO₃(aq) [Sulphurous acid]
6. Conclusion: Non-metals react with oxygen to produce non-metallic oxides (such as SO₂) which dissolve in water to form acids, turning blue litmus red and proving their acidic nature.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Acidic anhydrides dissolve in water to generate hydronium ions.
Q60 • Numerical Metals Above Hydrogen Count
medium 1 Marks
Number of metals which lie above hydrogen out of the following is: Sodium, lead, copper, platinum, zinc, mercury.
Model Textbook Answer
3
Examiner & Concept Tip: Sodium (Na), Lead (Pb), and Zinc (Zn) lie above hydrogen in the reactivity series. Copper (Cu), Platinum (Pt), and Mercury (Hg) lie below hydrogen. Total count = 3.

easy 1 Marks

Model Textbook Answer
4
Examiner & Concept Tip: The balanced chemical equation for the oxidation of sodium is: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O. Comparing with the formula, x = 4 and x/2 = 2.
Q62 • Numerical Basic Oxide Forming Elements Count
medium 1 Marks
Number of elements which form basic oxide is: Magnesium, aluminium, carbon, sulphur, iron, potassium, zinc.
Model Textbook Answer
3
Examiner & Concept Tip: Magnesium, iron, and potassium form basic oxides (MgO, Fe₂O₃/FeO, K₂O). Aluminium and zinc form amphoteric oxides (Al₂O₃, ZnO). Carbon and sulphur form acidic oxides. Total basic oxide-forming elements = 3 (or 5 if amphoteric metallic oxides are grouped under general basic metal oxides).
Q63 • Numerical Elements Inactive with Boiling Water
medium 1 Marks
Number of elements which will not react even with boiling water is: Sodium, iron, zinc, copper, magnesium, silver.
Model Textbook Answer
4
Examiner & Concept Tip: Sodium reacts with cold water; magnesium reacts with hot/boiling water. Iron and zinc react only with steam (not liquid boiling water); copper and silver do not react at all. Therefore, iron, zinc, copper, and silver (4 elements) will not react with liquid boiling water.
Q64 • Numerical Feasible Reactions Count
hard 1 Marks
Number of possible reactions out of the following is: 1. Cu + 2AgNO₃ → 2Ag + Cu(NO₃)₂ 2. Cu + ZnSO₄ → CuSO₄ + Zn 3. Mg + CuSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Cu 4. Zn + PbSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Pb
Model Textbook Answer
3
Examiner & Concept Tip: Reactions 1 (Cu > Ag), 3 (Mg > Cu), and 4 (Zn > Pb) are feasible displacement reactions. Reaction 2 is not feasible because Cu is less reactive than Zn. Total possible reactions = 3.

Assertion & Reason #1 Unanswered
Assertion: Iron is found in free state in nature.
Reason: Iron is not highly reactive metal.
Official Solution (D):
Iron is moderately reactive and readily reacts with oxygen and moisture; hence it never occurs in the free state in nature (it occurs as oxides/haematite).
Assertion & Reason #2 Unanswered
Assertion: Zinc is used in galvanisation of iron.
Reason: Its coating on iron articles increases their life by protecting them from rusting.
Official Solution (A):
Zinc coating shields iron from air and moisture, and corrodes sacrificially to preserve the underlying iron.
Assertion & Reason #3 Unanswered
Assertion: Copper cannot displace hydrogen from acids.
Reason: It lies above hydrogen in the reactivity series.
Official Solution (C):
Assertion is true (copper does not displace H₂ from dilute non-oxidising acids). The reason is false because copper lies *below* hydrogen in the reactivity series.
Assertion & Reason #4 Unanswered
Assertion: Aluminium appears dull in colour and does not react with water, acids or alkalies.
Reason: It has a protective layer of oxide on it.
Official Solution (A):
A dense, protective film of aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) forms on the surface of aluminium, rendering it relatively inert to normal atmospheric exposure.
Assertion & Reason #5 Unanswered
Assertion: If a piece of copper is placed in silver nitrate solution, the solution becomes blue.
Reason: Displacement reaction takes place and copper goes into the solution.
Official Solution (A):
Cu + 2AgNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ [Blue] + 2Ag. Copper displaces silver and enters solution as blue hydrated Cu²⁺ ions.
Assertion & Reason #6 Unanswered
Assertion: On beating with the help of a hammer, coal is converted into small pieces and finally into a powder.
Reason: Coal is made up of carbon which is malleable in nature.
Official Solution (C):
Coal shatters upon hammering because carbon is a non-metal that is *brittle*, not malleable.
Assertion & Reason #7 Unanswered
Assertion: Most of the metals can be beaten into sheets.
Reason: Most of the metals are ductile.
Official Solution (B):
Both statements are true. However, being beaten into sheets is due to *malleability*, not ductility (which refers to being drawn into wires).
Assertion & Reason #8 Unanswered
Assertion: Graphite is a non-metal.
Reason: It is the only non-metal which is good conductor of electricity.
Official Solution (B):
Both statements are true. Graphite is an allotropic form of carbon (non-metal) and conducts electricity due to free pi electrons, but conducting electricity is not the reason it is classified as a non-metal.
Assertion & Reason #9 Unanswered
Assertion: A solution of carbon dioxide in water turns red litmus blue.
Reason: Carbon dioxide is basic oxide.
Official Solution (D):
Carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid in water (CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃), which is an acidic oxide that turns blue litmus red, not red litmus blue.
Assertion & Reason #10 Unanswered
Assertion: Copper and aluminium are used to make electric wires.
Reason: Copper and aluminium are good conductors of electricity.
Official Solution (A):
Copper and aluminium possess high electrical conductivity and ductility, making them ideal for manufacturing electrical transmission wires.

High-Stakes Exam Defense

Exam Traps, Pitfalls & 3D Flashcards

Avoid the 8 common errors where CBSE & Olympiad candidates lose marks, plus 16 high-yield flip flashcards.

!

The 8 Fatal Exam Traps (Never Lose These Marks)

Trap 1: Amphoteric Oxide Product Names
Wrong: Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH ➔ NaAlO + H₂

Correct: Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH ➔ 2NaAlO₂ (Sodium Aluminate) + H₂O. Notice water (H₂O) is formed, NOT hydrogen gas!

Trap 2: Nitric Acid (HNO₃) H₂ Release
Wrong: Zn + 2HNO₃ ➔ Zn(NO₃)₂ + H₂ ↑

Correct: HNO₃ oxidises H₂ into H₂O! Zn produces NO₂ or NO. Only Mg and Mn produce H₂ with ~1% very dilute HNO₃.

Trap 3: Steam vs Water Hydroxide Mistake
Wrong: Fe + H₂O (steam) ➔ Fe(OH)₂ + H₂

Correct: Steam reacts with red-hot iron to form Magnetic Iron Oxide (Fe₃O₄): 3Fe + 4H₂O (g) ➔ Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂. No hydroxides form with steam!

Trap 4: 24-Carat vs 22-Carat Composition
Wrong: 22-carat gold contains 22% pure gold.

Correct: Carats are measured out of 24 parts! 22-carat = (22/24) × 100 = 91.6% pure gold + 8.4% copper/silver.

Trap 5: Scratched Galvanised Iron
Wrong: Once scratched, the exposed iron rusts immediately.

Correct: Zinc has higher oxidation potential (Zn > Fe). Zinc oxidises preferentially (sacrificial protection), saving the iron from rusting!

Trap 6: Aqua Regia Ratio Inversion
Wrong: 1 part HCl : 3 parts HNO₃

Correct: 3 parts Concentrated HCl : 1 part Concentrated HNO₃. (Memory trick: HCl has 3 letters in H-C-l, so it gets 3 parts!).

Trap 7: Rust Formula Hydration Number
Wrong: Formula of rust is Fe₂O₃ or FeO

Correct: Rust is hydrated: Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. The number of water molecules (x) is variable depending on air humidity.

Trap 8: Brass vs Bronze Composition
Wrong: Brass is Cu + Sn; Bronze is Cu + Zn

Correct: Brass = Cu + Zn (Zinc). Bronze = Cu + Sn (Tin). (Memory trick: Bronze does NOT have Zinc!).

Amphoteric Oxides & Dual Acid-Base Reactions

Mastering the balanced equations of Al₂O₃ and ZnO reacting with both hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide.

Key Conceptual Anchors
  • Al₂O₃ + 6HCl ➔ 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O (Acts as Base).
  • Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH ➔ 2NaAlO₂ (Sodium Aluminate) + H₂O (Acts as Acid).
  • ZnO forms Sodium Zincate (Na₂ZnO₂) with hot concentrated NaOH.

Kinetics Module #3

Reactivity Series & Single Displacement Dynamics

How the electropositivity ladder governs single displacement in aqueous solutions and the thermite welding reaction.

Key Conceptual Anchors
  • Mnemonic: Please Stop Calling Me A Careless Zebra Instead Try Learning...
  • Fe in CuSO₄: Blue turns pale green; reddish-brown copper deposits on nail.
  • Thermite: Fe₂O₃ + 2Al produces white-hot liquid molten iron for railway welding.

Mechanisms Module #4

Metal Reactions with Cold Water, Hot Water & Steam

Why K & Na catch fire in cold water, why Ca & Mg float, and why Fe, Al, and Zn require superheated steam.

Key Conceptual Anchors
  • K & Na: Highly exothermic; evolved H₂ immediately ignites with lilac/yellow flame.
  • Ca & Mg: Float on surface because buoyant H₂ gas bubbles stick to metal chunks.
  • Steam: 3Fe + 4H₂O (g) ➔ Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂ (forms magnetic oxide, not hydroxide).

Allotropy Module #5

Non-Metals Chemistry & Carbon Allotropes

The structural distinction between 3D tetrahedral diamond, 2D planar graphite, and hollow spherical buckyballs (C₆₀).

Key Conceptual Anchors
  • Diamond: sp³ rigid 3D lattice, hardest natural substance, electrical insulator.
  • Graphite: sp² planar sheets held by weak van der Waals forces; conducts electricity.
  • Fullerene: C₆₀ truncated icosahedron with 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons.

Corrosion Module #6

Electrochemistry of Iron Rusting & Prevention

Why rusting requires both oxygen and moisture, the formula of rust, and why galvanised iron stays protected when scratched.

Key Conceptual Anchors
  • Rust Formula: Hydrated Iron(III) Oxide: Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.
  • Silver: Forms black Ag₂S; Copper forms green basic copper carbonate patina.
  • Galvanisation: Sacrificial anodic protection by zinc layer.

Engineering Module #7

The Commercial Alloys Master Guide

Composition, properties, and applications of Brass, Bronze, Solder, Stainless Steel, Duralumin, and 22-Carat Gold.

Key Conceptual Anchors
  • Brass: Cu (70%) + Zn (30%) • Utensils and musical acoustic brass instruments.
  • Bronze: Cu (90%) + Sn (10%) • Medals, coins, and heavy statues.
  • Solder: Pb (50%) + Sn (50%) • Low melting point (183°C) for circuit joints.

Ancient Science Module #8

The Mystery of the Rustless Iron Pillar of Delhi

Scientific investigation into how the 1,600-year-old Gupta period pillar resisted monsoons without rusting.

Key Conceptual Anchors
  • Height: 7.2m, Weight: > 6 tonnes; forged c. 400 CE during Gupta Empire.
  • High phosphorus in iron slag catalyzed a self-healing misawite (α-FeOOH) coating.
  • Proof of sophisticated ancient Indian metallurgical furnace techniques.
